opus-5.5.text:
Cash is a terrible long-term investment. I've said for a long time that cash is trash, and what I mean is that when you look at the return on cash after inflation and after taxes, you're typically not building wealth. You may be earning an interest rate that looks attractive, but what matters is what that money can buy. If you're getting, say, 4 or 5 percent and inflation is running close to that, then you pay taxes on the interest, you're treading water or actually losing buying power over time.

And that's not an accident. When you look at history, governments with a lot of debt have a strong incentive to keep interest rates low relative to inflation, because that's how the debt burden gets eased. So the holder of cash and debt assets is on the wrong side of that. Over the long sweep of history, currencies have repeatedly lost value, and that's one of the biggest risks people underappreciate, because they think of cash as the safe asset. It feels safe because the number on the statement doesn't go down, but its real value does.

Now, that doesn't mean you should hold none. Cash is useful for liquidity, for covering your near-term expenses, for having dry powder when opportunities come along, and for reducing volatility in a downturn. But that's a tactical role. It's not a way to store and grow wealth over the long term.

For the long term, the most important thing is to have a well-diversified portfolio, with assets that do well in different environments, including some that protect you when currencies are being devalued, like gold and inflation-linked bonds, along with quality equities and a mix across countries and currencies. So hold cash for what you need it for, but don't mistake it for a safe long-term investment.

r001.rationale: The response calls cash a poor long-term investment and explains its potential loss of buying power, but it does not say its long-term return is almost guaranteed to be the worst.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I've always said that cash is not a safe investment, and most people have it backwards. They think of cash as the safe thing, and they think of everything else as risky. But what's safe? Safe is that you preserve your buying power over time. And cash, over time, has been a terrible investment, because it's taxed by inflation.

Think about it this way. The money that you hold in a deposit or a money market fund, you're getting an interest rate. Now, that interest rate, after inflation and after taxes, has historically been negative or close to zero for most of the last hundred years. So you don't lose it in a dramatic way. You lose it quietly. You lose it a little bit every year. And it's the quietness of it that fools people. Nobody sees cash fall thirty percent in a day, so they feel safe, but if you look at what a dollar bought in 1970 versus what it buys today, you've lost the great majority of your purchasing power.

And there's a deeper thing to understand here, which is how money works. Central banks, when they're in trouble, when there's too much debt, they print money. That's what they do, and they've always done it, going back thousands of years. Every reserve currency in history has eventually been devalued. So when you hold cash, you are essentially holding a liability of a government that has every incentive, when things get difficult, to make that cash worth less. That's not a conspiracy, that's just the mechanics of the debt cycle.

Now, I want to be clear. That doesn't mean you shouldn't hold any cash. There are times, and we've had some recently, when short-term rates are high relative to inflation, and cash is okay for a period. And you need liquidity. You need to be able to pay your bills, you need to be able to meet obligations without being forced to sell things at the wrong moment. So cash as a tactical position, as a place to wait, as liquidity, fine. But cash as a long-term investment, as a place where you put your wealth and expect it to be there in twenty or thirty years with the same buying power, no. That's one of the biggest mistakes people make.

What I'd rather see people do is have a well-diversified portfolio, a balanced mix of assets that do well in different environments, so that you're not betting on any one thing. Some stocks, some bonds, some gold, some inflation-linked assets. Because the one thing I know is that I don't know what's going to happen, and neither does anybody else, and the portfolio has to be built to survive that uncertainty. Cash doesn't survive it. Cash just erodes.

r001.rationale: The response says cash has historically been a poor long-term investment and erodes purchasing power, but it does not state that short-term interest-bearing cash is almost guaranteed to have the worst long-term investment return.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between safety in nominal terms and safety in purchasing power. Cash in a deposit or a money market fund can feel safe because the balance doesn’t fluctuate very much, and you’re earning interest. But the question is: after taxes and inflation, what can that money buy?

And the interest rate you’re receiving today isn’t locked in for the long term. When those short-term investments mature, you have to reinvest at whatever rate is available then.

So cash has a purpose. You need liquidity to meet your obligations, and it gives you flexibility to take advantage of opportunities. But I wouldn’t confuse that with being a great long-term investment. Whether it’s attractive depends on its return relative to inflation and other assets. For long-term wealth, I would want a well-diversified portfolio that can perform across different economic environments.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that cash may not be a great long-term investment, but does not state that it is almost guaranteed to have the worst long-term return.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between safety in nominal terms and safety in purchasing power. With cash, you can feel safe because the number in your account doesn’t go down, and you’re collecting interest. But the question is: what are you earning after inflation and taxes? If that return is negative, your money is losing purchasing power even though the balance is rising.

Cash has a purpose. It gives you liquidity, it allows you to meet obligations, and it gives you the ability to take advantage of opportunities. And there are periods when the interest rate makes it attractive. But I wouldn’t confuse that with a great long-term investment. I’d want a diversified portfolio of assets that can preserve and grow purchasing power through different economic environments.

r001.rationale: The response questions cash as a long-term investment and notes it can lose purchasing power, but does not state that short-term interest-bearing cash is almost guaranteed to have the worst long-term investment return.
